What is Graduation Coaching?

In Search of the 'Magic Ingredients' and Implications for Scaling

By Mahreen Khan (University of Oxford) and Patricia Andrews-Fearon (The Agency Fund) · Draft Date: August 2026

“[S]omehow that ‘touch point’ is key…some person is with you for two years, even if maybe now over the phone [and] occasionally in group settings; you have someone to troubleshoot with if things go wrong - it can adjust to a certain extent and it complements you on that behavioral change - nudging you to keep going and not to give up, right? Somewhere in that, I think, lies the magic…And I think the good news is that it is not actually a job that requires any degrees or any ‘skilling’ or anything. It requires empathy, it requires listening skills, and so on, right?”

Implementer interview #1

Executive Summary

Coaching is widely regarded as one of the defining features of the graduation approach to extreme poverty. Often described as the “human touch” within graduation programming, coaching helps ensure that asset transfers, training, savings support, and other program inputs translate into sustained changes in participants’ livelihoods and wellbeing. As graduation programs have expanded beyond their origins in Bangladesh and have been adapted by NGOs, governments, and hybrid delivery partnerships, coaching has evolved to accommodate the array of local needs, institutional capacities, participant profiles, and resource constraints. These coaching adaptations are not merely operational details. Choices about whom to recruit as coaches, how to train them, how frequently they meet participants, whether coaching is delivered individually or in groups, and how digital tools are used all reflect implicit assumptions about how coaching contributes to participant outcomes. Making these assumptions explicit lets researchers test which coaching features matter most, and helps implementers and funders judge where trade-offs are safe, and where innovation can make coaching more cost-effective to scale.

This report maps the current landscape of coaching implementation across graduation programs and examines what these implementation choices reveal about the possible mechanisms through which coaching works. Every major design choice, which includes whom to recruit, what to train coaches on, how often they visit, and whether to substitute technology for human contact, encodes an implicit assumption about why coaching works. The objective is not to prescribe a single model of coaching, but to provide a clearer framework for understanding the trade-offs involved in designing and funding coaching at scale. Naming these assumptions reveals the different theories of change at work and turns the trade-offs into questions a research agenda can test.

Drawing on organizational behavior and mentoring scholarship, supplemented by behavioral and development economics, we characterize graduation coaching as a hybrid developmental relationship. We distinguish four broad functions that coaches may perform. First, coaches may serve an aspirational function by shifting how participants see themselves and their futures. Second, they serve a behavioral function by supporting planning, accountability, skill-building and follow-through. Third, they serve a relational function by providing trust, encouragement, emotional support, and connection to wider social and institutional networks. Finally, they may also serve an administrative function through case management, monitoring, record-keeping and referral tracking.

In practice, these functions often overlap. A single coaching interaction may help a participant solve an immediate problem, reinforce a savings commitment, provide reassurance after a setback, and update program records. Distinguishing them conceptually is useful because each function depends on different ingredients to work: the aspirational and relational functions, for example, may depend heavily on recruiting coaches with a particular profile or set of socio-emotional skills, while the accountability function may depend on the frequency and consistency of contact. They therefore differ in how readily group delivery can substitute for one-on-one coaching, or technology for the in-person human coach.

Our analysis of implementation choices, drawn from key informant interviews and program documentation, yields four main findings:

  • Implementers consistently recruit for relational competencies over formal credentials. Empathy, listening skills, communication, local embeddedness, and the ability to build trust are often prioritized, reflecting a widely held view among implementers that coaching works in part through trust, encouragement, and sustained relational engagement. At the same time, the evidence base remains limited on which specific coach attributes matter most for which participant outcomes.

  • Coaching intensity and delivery format are more flexible than once believed. The strongest comparative evidence currently available, from Uganda, the Philippines, and Bangladesh, indicates that group-based coaching can produce outcomes comparable to individual coaching on consumption, income, and asset value, while reducing implementation costs by roughly 15 to 20 percent. This does not imply that individual contact is unnecessary. Rather, it suggests that programs may be able to use group-based delivery as a default model, while reserving more intensive individual support for participants facing higher levels of vulnerability or more complex needs.

  • Technology is being used to augment rather than replace human coaching. Digital tools can support case management, data collection, training, supervisory feedback, content delivery, and just-in-time problem solving. These uses can reduce administrative burden on coaches and improve consistency at scale. However, implementers interviewed for this report did not advocate fully replacing embodied relational or motivational support with digital channels. The current evidence base does not yet establish where the boundary lies between functions that can be digitized and those that still require direct human engagement.

  • Cross-program learning is constrained by inconsistent data. Programs often do not report comparable information on caseloads, contact frequency, session duration, coach compensation, training intensity, attrition, or per-participant coaching costs. This limits the ability of funders and researchers to assess cost-effectiveness, compare delivery models, or learn from the substantial variation already present across the field.

From these findings we offer nine policy recommendations for implementers and funders, ranging from designing programs around an explicit theory of how coaching changes behavior, through recruiting for relational competencies, defaulting to group-based delivery with individual follow-up for higher-need participants, treating technology as augmentation, and investing in coach well-being as a sustainability issue, to standardizing cross-program cost reporting and prioritizing research that identifies coaching's active ingredients.

The central message of this report is that coaching remains a valuable and distinctive component of graduation programming, but that its design rests on assumptions about why it works that are rarely made explicit—and rarely tested. The field has accumulated substantial practical experience across diverse contexts. The next step is to use that experience more systematically: to clarify which coaching functions matter most in which settings, to identify which elements can be adapted without compromising effectiveness, and to support implementers and funders in making transparent, context-sensitive design choices as graduation programs continue to scale.

Introduction

“Hands-on” coaching features as one of the most critical components of economic inclusion programs modeled after the BRAC graduation approach (BRAC, 2015) – one of the most effective evidence-based approaches to large-scale poverty reduction.

“Graduation” programs are designed to build enduring economic resilience for participants through a comprehensive, multi-dimensional approach. These “wrap around” programs can be built onto the scaffolding of standard social protection schemes by incorporating a time-bound, sequential provision of assets, life-skills, technical training and socio-emotional support. Consequently, they merge the material “basic needs” component of traditional social protection, such as cash and asset-based transfers, with a carefully sequenced curriculum to facilitate the sustained utilization of the asset spread over a delivery period of 18 to 36 months (see Figure 1). The original graduation model, developed in Bangladesh around 2002, equipped its “ultra poor” participants with skills to continue improving their situation beyond the program— so they could "graduate" out of extreme poverty. Notably, the coaching component was widely credited as the foundation of the program's success — providing participants with sustained, personalized human support throughout the entire duration of the program.

“Strengthening coaching systems through investments in workforce capability, supervision, and adaptive delivery mechanisms represents one of the highest-leverage opportunities for improving programme outcomes and achieving sustainable impact at scale.” (Ouko & Abrams, 2026, p. 5)”

In the two decades since the inception of graduation in Bangladesh, this template has been translated and adapted for different target populations at varying stages of economic development in a multitude of contexts. It has been taken up by governments, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), or a combination of the two. This means that while the basic notion of graduation (poverty alleviation through a sequenced and multi-dimensional approach) remains constant, the contents and combinations of these components have evolved in diverse ways.

The question of what makes coaching effective is not merely academic. Recent experimental evidence suggests that the psychological and relational dimensions of support programs — aspiration, agency, and self-efficacy — may be more potent drivers of long-term outcomes than previously assumed (Bossuroy et al., 2022). If the “active ingredient” in coaching is primarily aspirational, then coaching might be delivered effectively through lighter-touch, more scalable models. Two recent randomized trials make this concrete. In rural Ethiopia, a single screening of short documentaries featuring relatable local role models raised household labor supply, agricultural investment, spending on children's schooling and durable asset holdings five years later, with treated households reporting higher lifetime aspirations relative to both a placebo and a control group (Bernard et al., 2026). Meanwhile, in Kenya, an eighty-minute aspirations-and-planning workshop raised productive investment, revenue, consumption and asset value at seventeen months, and nearly paid for itself in consumption gains alone over that period (Orkin et al., 2023). Notably, the same trial finds that the workshop combined with a large cash transfer produced effects similar to the cash transfer alone, suggesting that improving economic conditions can activate the same aspirational process. If the active ingredient is behavioral, the implications for scale depend on which part of that function does the work. Accountability and motivational support may be relatively low-bandwidth, and there is reason to think they can be sustained through group delivery, peer structures or digital check-ins. Technical skill transfer is less easily standardized and remains dependent on coach competence, so scaling it without dilution is considerably harder.

The coaching component is what distinguishes graduation programs from other cash- and asset-transfer models of economic inclusion—but it is also the component most open to interpretation, and therefore the most malleable. This malleability is double-edged. On one hand, it is what allows coaching to travel: the early pilots of 2006–15, led by CGAP and the Ford Foundation, closely mimicked BRAC's Bangladesh model, but subsequent iterations have adapted coaching to the resources and innovative capacity of each implementing organization. This flexibility is essential for government-led scale-up, where large national or regional social protection programs must fit coaching to their institutional constraints while meeting the distinct needs of specific sub-populations—women, children, youth, and refugees. On the other hand, the same flexibility makes coaching vulnerable: when resources are constrained, it can be pared back in ways that risk diluting its most essential ingredients. The difficulty is that the field cannot yet reliably distinguish productive adaptation from harmful dilution, because it does not know which ingredients are essential in the first place.

This report aims to map the landscape of coaching implementation across graduation programs and surfaces a central finding: every major design choice reflects an underlying assumption about why coaching works. Because the field does not yet know the answer to that question, programs are in effect testing different theories of change in parallel without always recognizing it. By making these assumptions explicit, we aim to help researchers design studies that test which components of coaching drive outcomes, and to help implementers make more deliberate choices about the trade-offs they face when scaling. Specifically, we will review i) key coaching functions; ii) coach profiles and selection processes; iii) coaching contents; iv) the design of coach training; v) cost-saving innovations from the field; and vi) key considerations for scaling in light of programmatic trade-offs.

Conceptual Foundations

The coaching component of graduation programs has, until recently, been described primarily through the rich field-based intuition of implementers and captured in evocative language about "magic sauce," "X-factors," and "the human touch." While this descriptive vocabulary has served the field well as a shorthand, it has also obscured three questions that any policy analyst, and any future evaluation, must confront: 1) What is “coaching” in the graduation context? 2) What are the core functions of coaches? and 3) How might these activities produce lasting change for participants? This section addresses these questions by drawing on theory and evidence from across the behavioral sciences, but particularly from organizational behavior (OB) and mentoring scholarship, and supplemented by behavioral and development economics, as well as social psychology where relevant.1

What is “coaching” in the graduation context?

The terms "coaching" and "mentoring" are used interchangeably across graduation program documentation, and indeed across the broader economic inclusion literature. However, organizational behavior research has long treated them as analytically distinct constructs, and that distinction is consequential for how graduation programs are designed and evaluated.

In its canonical formulation, mentoring is a relational, developmental, typically longer-term, and often dyadic, relationship between a more experienced individual and a protégé, oriented toward the protégé's overall growth across career and psychosocial domains (Kram, 1985; Ragins & Kram, 2007). Coaching, by contrast, is more commonly described as a task-focused, performance-oriented, shorter-term relationship aimed at building specific competencies (D'Abate, Eddy & Tannenbaum, 2003; Haggard et al., 2011). Subsequent scholarship has emphasized that the empirical referents of these terms overlap substantially, that the boundary is more porous than early definitions suggested, and that the distinction is best treated as one of functional emphasis rather than discrete category (Haggard et al., 2011).

Graduation "coaching" maps imperfectly onto either paradigm. It runs for eighteen to thirty-six months, which is closer to the mentoring end of the duration spectrum; it is explicitly developmental and frequently psychosocial in content; and the canonical BRAC model envisaged coaches as embarking on their own "parallel journey of behavioural change" — a description that aligns far more closely with mentoring's role-modeling dimension than with task-focused coaching. At the same time, graduation coaching incorporates structured curricula, behavioral targets, and skill-building modules that resemble the goal-directed, performance-oriented work characteristic of coaching in the narrow sense. We treat graduation coaching as a hybrid developmental relationship drawing functional elements from both constructs, and we retain the field's standard term "coaching" for continuity. The implication, however, is that programs face a real design choice about which function to prioritize — and, as we show in subsequent sections, different implementers are implicitly making different bets.


What are the coaches’ core functions? And how might these support lasting change for the ultra-poor?

Once graduation coaching is recognized as a hybrid relationship with multiple distinct functions, a second question follows: which functions are actually doing the work? Drawing on mentoring scholarship, which has long disaggregated the mentor role into functional categories (Kram, 1985; Higgins & Kram, 2001; Eby et al., 2013), we distinguish four broad functional clusters (three psychosocial and one operational) that graduation coaches fulfill. Though these four clusters are analytically distinct, we do not yet know whether they can operate independently in practice, or which might be most responsible for coaching's effects. One way to understand the distinct but interlocking nature of the psychosocial functions of coaching is to ask: what does escaping extreme poverty demand of participants? — more specifically, what beliefs, skills, practices, and connections must be cultivated to "get up and stay up" economically?

First, a participant must be able to imagine a better future and believe it is possible for someone like them (the aspirational function). Second, they must be able to set specific goals and chart a viable path toward these goals -- articulating the specific steps and skills that will lead out of poverty (the behavioral function). Third, they must believe they can walk that path and be able to draw on encouragement and social support along the way (the relational function).

A note on what follows: these four functions of coaching are analytically separable but operationally entangled. A single home visit may, in the space of an hour, rekindle a participant's sense of possibility, hold her to last month's savings commitment, offer warmth after a setback, and update a case file. The point of disaggregating them is not to claim that coaches switch between discrete functional modes, nor to suggest that the functions should be uncoupled in practice. Rather, it is to make visible that coaching programs invest in some mix of these four functions but rarely specify which.

The aspirational function concerns the first link in this chain: whether a participant can imagine a better future and believe it is attainable for someone like them. Development economics treats the absence of this belief as a behavioral poverty trap — low aspirations depress the effort and investment needed to escape poverty, which in turn reinforces low aspirations (Ray, 2006; Dalton, Ghosal & Mani, 2016). Moreover, people calibrate their aspirations -- what they believe is possible for them -- by observing others similar to, and just ahead of, themselves. In other words, access to relatable role models (or lack thereof) can critically shape their “aspiration windows.” This gives the aspirational function of coaches two distinguishable components — widening the horizon of imagined futures, and supplying a proximate, credible example that the horizon applies to "someone like me" (Kram, 1985; Scandura & Ragins, 1993). Coaches plausibly act on both: through future-oriented conversation and goal setting, and by serving as visible role models whose own progression demonstrates that change is possible.

Notably, some of the strongest evidence that this channel does independent work comes from interventions that target aspirations with no coach at all. Exposure to a short documentary featuring people from similar backgrounds who had escaped poverty through their own efforts raised aspirations and educational investment, and five years later recipients had accumulated substantially more productive and household assets (Bernard et al., 2026); light-touch psychological interventions combining role models with goal-setting have likewise shifted real economic behavior (Orkin et al., 2023).

The behavioral/skill-building function concerns the second link: translating aspirational intentions into action, sustaining effort, and acquiring the specific skills required to follow this path. These include planning (helping participants learn to sequence concrete steps towards their goals), accountability (check-ins that maintain commitment in the face of competing demands), and targeted skill-building (e.g., animal husbandry techniques). Where the aspirational function addresses a participant’s motivation to act, the behavioral function addresses the well-documented gap between intention and behavior. On this point, behavioral science offers a broad evidence-based toolkit for closing this intention–action gap, much of it resembling what coaches already do. For example, research demonstrates that specific, proximate goals outperform vague ones (Locke & Latham, 2002; Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006) and external commitment and accountability structures can help mitigate "present bias,” the human tendency to prioritize short-term instead of longer-term rewards (Laibson, 1997; O'Donoghue & Rabin, 1999; Bryan, Karlan & Nelson, 2010). In this way, coaches may help participants establish new habits and self-regulatory skills, and even a new sense of identity as participants come to see themselves as the kind of person who saves, plans, or runs a small enterprise (Akerlof & Kranton, 2000, 2010).

Evidence that this channel does independent work also comes from interventions delivered without a personal coach. Simple reminders can increase savings (Karlan et al., 2016); plan-making prompts and implementation-intention exercises can raise follow-through on financial and health behaviors (Gollwitzer & Sheeran, 2006); and commitment devices increase savings among the poor (Ashraf, Karlan & Yin, 2006). Across business-training trials, short courses raise microenterprise profits, with psychology-based curricula teaching personal initiative and simplified rules of thumb outperforming conventional instruction (Drexler, Fischer & Schoar, 2014; Campos et al., 2017; McKenzie, 2021), and classroom financial education shifts budgeting and saving behaviors (Kaiser et al., 2022). However, critical caveats apply: First, evidence from interventions with existing microenterprise owners may fail to generalize to ultra-poor households who face materially different constraints; Second, skill-based trainings may still require other behavioral supports to produce durable effects. For example, the same personal-initiative curriculum that produced durable profit gains in a Togo study where trainers made monthly follow-up visits (Campos et al., 2025), produced short-term but not long-term gains in Jamaica (Ubfal et al., 2022) – a decay that the authors attribute to the absence of follow-up. Third, these effects also appear gendered: the Togo profit gains persisted over seven years only among men, with women's effects flat or declining (Campos et al., 2025), and Jamaica's short-term gains were likewise concentrated among men (Ubfal et al., 2022). This may reflect the individualistic framing of personal-initiative curricula rather than a limit on the channel itself — among ultra-poor Nigerien women, a culturally attuned "relational agency" exercise improved economic outcomes over twelve months while an equivalent Western-derived personal-agency exercise did not move the economic composite (Thomas et al., 2025).

The relational function concerns the emotional and social resources the coach provides — warmth, validation, trust, and the felt sense that someone credible believes the participant can succeed. In the belief chain, this is what converts a viable plan into sustained action: the conviction that "I am capable of walking this path," and the access to support when setbacks threaten to knock participants off track. Several literatures converge on why this matters. Self-efficacy theory identifies credible verbal persuasion from a trusted figure (i.e. a coach’s affirmations and encouragement) as one of the four canonical sources of efficacy beliefs (Bandura, 1977, 1997). Mentoring research consistently finds that psychosocial support — counselling, acceptance, encouragement — predicts protégé outcomes independent of task-focused help (Kram, 1985; Allen et al., 2004; Eby et al., 2013). Self-determination theory treats relatedness as a basic psychological need underpinning durable motivation (Ryan & Deci, 2000), and the social-support literature shows that a trusted relationship buffers the stress of adverse events (Cohen & Wills, 1985) — precisely the shocks that can derail poverty-exit trajectories. The relational function may also support the accumulation of social capital through the coach's network (Higgins & Kram, 2001), helping to forge the economic and social connections that facilitate ongoing development.

Administrative functions, which include case management, record-keeping, monitoring and evaluation, are operationally important and absorb significant coach time, but are analytically distinct from the developmental functions above. These four clusters are neither mutually exclusive nor exhaustive, and they are unlikely to operate independently in practice — relational trust may, for example, be a precondition for aspirational influence and aspirational shifts may sustain the behavioral follow-through that planning support attempts to scaffold. But they are, nevertheless, conceptually distinct, and separating them reveals something the field has left implicit: programs facing similar constraints prioritize different functions — and each choice reflects an unstated theory of why coaching matters.

Revealing Implicit Priorities

These presumed mechanisms also imply different answers to questions about which coaching inputs might be reduced or altered while still maintaining its core efficacy. Questions such as: How much contact is enough? How far can technology replace human contact? Does who the coach is matter more than how often they show up? Rather than adjudicate between these here, we briefly outline how assumptions about the importance of each coaching function might influence implementation trade-offs, and then we return to these themes in each empirical section, making visible which mechanism a given implementation choice quietly prioritizes.

If the aspirational function is a primary mechanism, then a coach's background, social proximity to the participant's starting point, and visible progression should matter more than the technical content they deliver. More provocatively, much of the function may be deliverable through far cheaper means. Structured aspirational exercises can be delivered through one-off group workshops (Bossuroy et al., 2022; Orkin et al., 2023). Role-model stories and peer role-model exposure (Beaman et al., 2012; Macours & Vakis, 2016; Riley, 2024) can help expand people's aspirational windows (Ray, 2006; Genicot & Ray, 2017), especially where role models share a relatable background, modeling how to begin from a similar economic starting point (Nguyen, 2008) and how to aspire in ways that are wise to salient local norms and cultural values (Walton & Wilson, 2018; Thomas et al., 2025). This evidence comes largely from educational settings, however, and its transfer to livelihood outcomes among ultra-poor adults has not been tested directly.

If the coaches’ behavioral/skill-building functions are driving impact, then the quality of the plan-making exercises, the frequency and consistency of contact — rather than the coach's personality or charisma — become the binding constraints, and much of the planning-and-accountability work may be deliverable through cheaper, scalable channels such as structured planning templates, SMS reminders, or one-off or periodic group sessions. The likely exception is livelihood-specific skill-building, which may require hands-on training from someone with both the relevant expertise and the ability to teach the skills effectively — making this the part of the behavioral function least amenable to digital substitution – particularly for the poorest households.

For the relational function, the implication for implementation runs opposite to the previous two functions. While the aspirational and behavioral channels draw their strongest evidence from interventions that work without a coach, suggesting they may be cheaply unbundled, the relational function does not come apart so cleanly. Its mechanism — a continuous, trusted relationship — is precisely what resists delivery by reminder, template, or one-off workshop, and it is the function many implementers are most adamant cannot be digitized. This makes the continuity and quality of the relationship, rather than contact frequency or content, the binding design parameters: empathy and embeddedness in recruitment, low coach turnover, and caseloads small enough to sustain trust. It also reframes the cost question. If the relational function is the irreducible human core of coaching, then the efficiency gains available elsewhere — automating administrative load, delivering aspirational and behavioral scaffolding through cheaper channels — matter largely because they protect scarce relational time rather than replace it.

The administrative functions are, in theory, largely substitutable by technology and non-coach personnel (insofar as administrative functions are separable from the psycho-social functions of coaches) and their inclusion in the coach role reflects organizational efficiency rather than any theoretical claim that a coach must deliver them.

Scope conditions and contextual moderators

The scholarship on coaching and mentorship reviewed above was developed largely in high-income organizational settings such as corporate mentoring relationships, professional development contexts, and structured workplace dyads. Its core constructs travel well to the graduation context, but several scope conditions warrant flagging. Coach-participant relationships in graduation programs are characterized by deeper structural power asymmetries than the workplace relationships from which mentoring theory was developed; they are typically more formal and externally initiated than the informal mentoring relationships that produce the strongest effects in the OB literature (Ragins & Cotton, 1999); they unfold across cultural settings in which the meaning of advice, accountability, and emotional disclosure may differ substantially from the contexts in which the underlying constructs were validated (Blake-Beard, Murrell & Thomas, 2007); and they place sustained emotional demands on coaches that the literature on emotional labor (Hochschild, 1983) suggests have implications for coach well-being and program sustainability. We treat these as boundary conditions on the applicability of these constructs rather than as reasons to discount them, and we return to coach-side considerations in our discussion of recruitment and of coaches as beneficiaries.

Report Methodology and Objectives

Research Design and Objectives

This report employs a qualitative, multi-method research design combining a systematic review of existing coaching practices within graduation programs, analysis of secondary data sources (evaluation reports, program documents, and research publications), and primary data collection through Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) with program stakeholders. The study was conducted with three objectives: (i) to provide a comprehensive overview of how the coaching component is designed and implemented across different contexts, deconstructing the roles and functions of coaches; (ii) to identify innovative practices with implications for reducing program costs and increasing scalability; and (iii) to generate actionable insights for implementing organizations and funders seeking to enhance program effectiveness through scaling.

Data Collection

Primary data were gathered through semi-structured KIIs with a purposefully selected sample of informants drawn from three stakeholder categories: program implementers, technical advisors to implementing organizations, and funders. Purposive sampling was employed to ensure representation across geographic regions, program maturity levels, and implementation modalities. Interviews were conducted remotely and followed a topic guide structured around the coaching lifecycle, which includes recruitment, training, content, delivery, supervision, and cost, while allowing for inductive exploration of emergent themes. The semi-structured format balanced comparability across informants with the flexibility to pursue context-specific issues in depth.

Secondary data sources comprised evaluation reports, program design documents, research publications, and internal analyzes produced by implementing organizations and research teams. A targeted literature review of existing evaluations was prepared in advance of the primary data collection to map the evidence base on coaching outcomes and to inform the interview topic guide.

Analytical Approach

The analysis followed an inductive, grounded-theory-informed approach (Strauss & Corbin, 1998; Gioia, Corley & Hamilton, 2013), proceeding through two distinct coding cycles. The analytical process began during data collection: after each interview, the researcher who conducted the interview wrote extensive analytical memos capturing initial impressions, emerging patterns, and points of convergence or divergence with prior interviews. These memos served as a bridge between raw data and formal coding, consistent with the reflexive memo-writing practices recommended in the grounded theory tradition (Charmaz, 2006).

In the first coding cycle, interview transcripts and memos were subjected to open coding to identify discrete features of coaching practice across contexts. Codes were generated inductively from the data rather than imposed from a pre-existing framework, though the researchers’ prior familiarity with the graduation model and the mentoring literature shaped the interpretive lens. Initial codes were organized into first-order categories capturing concrete coaching activities and design choices (e.g., “home visits,” “savings monitoring,” “referral to health services”). In the second coding cycle, first-order categories were grouped into higher-order themes through axial coding, producing the temporal sequencing of the coaching process that structures the report’s substantive sections. This two-stage process yielded the four core coaching functions presented in Figure 2, along with the cross-cutting themes of recruitment, training, supervision, and cost-effectiveness that organize the remaining sections.

Throughout the analytical process, the authors engaged in ongoing discussion to compare interpretations, resolve coding disagreements, and refine the emerging thematic structure. While formal inter-coder reliability metrics (e.g., Cohen’s kappa) were not computed, the iterative, team-based approach to interpretation provided a degree of analytical triangulation. Emerging themes were also cross-checked against the secondary data sources (program documents, evaluation reports) as a form of data triangulation, strengthening confidence that the patterns identified in the KIIs reflected genuine features of coaching practice rather than idiosyncratic informant perspectives. A draft of the report was additionally reviewed by two external peer reviewers, providing an independent check on the plausibility of the analytical framework and the coherence of the interpretation.

Limitations and Reflexivity

This report draws primarily on Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) with program implementers, technical advisors, and funders. While these stakeholders possess deep institutional knowledge of coaching design and implementation, their perspectives are shaped by organizational and professional incentives and realities. Implementers may present coaching models favorably, funders may emphasize features aligned with strategic priorities, and technical advisors are often embedded within the same ecosystem. As a result, each perspective introduces its own biases and limitations, including the potential understatement of implementation challenges or overstatement of program effectiveness. To mitigate this, interview findings were triangulated with secondary sources and evaluation evidence where available. However, these limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings.

A further limitation is the absence of direct participant and coach perspectives. The report therefore reflects the views of those who design, fund, oversee, and deliver coaching rather than those who receive it. This limits the study’s ability to assess how participants experience coaching relationships, how power dynamics shape interactions, or how coaches themselves perceive their workloads, motivations, and emotional demands. The organizational behavior literature emphasizes the value of a “mutuality perspective” that captures the experiences of both mentors and protégés (Dobrow et al., 2012). Future research would benefit from incorporating participant and coach voices directly.

The analytical approach followed established qualitative coding procedures, but formal inter-coder reliability metrics were not computed. While the research team engaged in iterative discussion and triangulation of findings, the thematic structure presented here should be understood as one defensible interpretation of the data rather than the only possible interpretation.

The findings are also not statistically generalizable. Informants and programs were purposely selected to capture diversity across contexts and implementation models rather than represent the full population of graduation programs globally. The findings should therefore be interpreted as analytical generalizations that may transfer to similar contexts rather than as representative estimates of global practice.

Finally, the research team’s professional proximity to organizations involved in promoting and studying the graduation approach provided contextual familiarity and access to informants but also introduced potential risks of confirmation bias. The analysis sought to mitigate this by actively identifying design trade-offs, unresolved questions, and areas where interview accounts diverged from available evaluation evidence. Nonetheless, the report should be read with awareness that it is situated within the broader graduation ecosystem.

What Coaches Actually Do: From Theory to Practice

“(T)he simplest and easiest and I think honest answer is that graduation and the accompaniment [coaching] that it advocates is really for people living in extreme poverty, who are unable to imagine how to make use of just an asset transfer: There is so much they need to do to even be able to imagine a different possibility beyond just getting basic consumption. The accompaniment (coaching) that graduation provides and that wraparound support is really necessary for the group living in extreme poverty.” - IMPL.1

Key Questions addressed in this section:

  • How has coaching changed since the graduation model spread beyond Bangladesh?

  • What do coaches do day-to-day, and how do those activities relate to the four functions introduced above?

Coaching is often referred to as the “magic sauce” or the “X-factor” for graduation by program practitioners and academics (Roelen, 2015, p. 1). At early stages of translation and adaptation, BRAC developed a toolkit for practitioners including governments and NGOs looking to implement and scale economic inclusion programs modeled after BRAC’s graduation approach. The toolkit described the coaching component as providing “encouragement, the instilling of discipline, education, skills and confidence and enabling access to resources” such that “By enabling participants to develop a vision of their future out of poverty, the (weekly) home visits are often credited as the most integral component essential to the success of the programme.” (BRAC, 2015, p. 67). The early templates recommended that coaches cover twelve key social and health issues during regular, weekly coaching visits (see details of recommended coaching topics in Table A2, in Appendix). Issues were selected based on the Bangladesh context and topics ranged from gender-based issues like early marriage and family planning to health issues like nutrition and disease prevention. These discussions were targeted to sync with overall graduation goals that included building well-being and resilience in the long-term for the most socio-economically vulnerable groups in the economy.

As graduation moved beyond Bangladesh, the topics and content of coaching sessions were the first elements to be adapted. But it soon became apparent that coaching was far harder to standardize than the rest of the package. Whereas programmatic features such as asset type, transfer size, and financial-literacy content could be specified with reasonable objectivity, coaching was interpreted with much greater heterogeneity and tailored closely to local idiosyncrasies. Current versions of the component are consequently shaped by a cluster of context-specific factors: program funding (the size, requirements, and timelines set by funders); the characteristics and geographic accessibility of target populations; the structure and capacity of implementing organizations; the degree of technological integration; and the locally available skillset of coaches. The level of control implementers exercise over coach selection, training, and delivery depends heavily on the type of local government or non-government partner involved in design and implementation. This report presents the heterogeneity that manifests from a series of constrained choices that, taken together, reveal what each program implicitly treats as the essence of coaching.

Operationalizing the Four Coaching Functions

The Conceptual Foundations distinguished four functions that coaches may perform: aspirational, behavioral, relational, and administrative. We demonstrate what each function looks like when a coach is in the room, and what the research suggests about how each might produce change. This matters because practitioners rarely describe their work in these terms. They speak instead of being an "accountability partner," a "touch-point" for training, or a "changemaker". While these are vivid and useful shorthand, they nonetheless blend several distinct functions together. Naming the functions underneath that vocabulary is what allows us to see how a single design choice quietly privileges one function over another.

The aspirational function

Interviews suggest that many implementers view coaching as more than a mechanism for transferring information or monitoring progress. Coaches are often expected to help participants imagine a future beyond immediate subsistence and to sustain confidence in the possibility of change over the course of the program. Several respondents described coaches as "changemakers" whose role extends beyond technical guidance to inspiring participants to articulate their aspirations, persist through setbacks, and maintain a longer-term perspective on their economic trajectories. This emphasis is reflected in recruitment practices described below by prioritizing coaches who are locally embedded and perceived as credible examples of personal advancement within their communities. In some cases, implementers explicitly valued coaches whose own experiences enabled them to connect with participants' circumstances and demonstrate that improvement is achievable.

These observations suggest that who the coach is — their background and relatability — matters more than the curriculum she delivers. This is the implicit logic behind recruiting locally embedded coaches who have themselves moved out of poverty, and it suggests that even relatively brief, well-judged interactions could carry an outsized impact.

The behavioral/skill-building function

Across programs, one of the most consistently cited roles of coaches is helping participants translate intentions into action. Implementers described coaches as accountability partners who support participants in setting specific goals, following through on commitments, and maintaining momentum throughout the program cycle. This includes activities such as monitoring savings behavior, reviewing business plans, tracking progress against livelihood goals, and helping participants navigate setbacks.

While the specific content of coaching varies considerably across contexts, the emphasis on regular follow-up is strikingly consistent. Many respondents highlighted the importance of repeated engagement over time, not only to reinforce technical training but also to sustain motivation and encourage participants to act on plans they have already developed. As one implementer noted, coaches play a critical role in “nudging you to keep going and not to give up.” The prominence of these activities helps explain why coaching frequency remains a central implementation decision. Programs that place greater emphasis on behavioral support tend to invest in structured follow-up processes, regular participant contact, and coaching content linked to concrete actions and milestones. This also helps explain growing interest in group-based delivery models, which may be able to preserve elements of coach accountability (or even amplify them through additional peer accountability) and follow-up while reducing costs. If behavioral support is the binding constraint, then the frequency and consistency of contact matter more than its intensity or duration. Critically, this has different implications for the two sides of the behavioral function. The accountability and motivational dimension (regular check-ins, reminders, encouragement to follow through) may be relatively cheap to sustain at scale, since it may depend on consistent low-bandwidth contact that could in principle be delivered through group sessions or digital channels such as SMS reminders rather than individual visits. The skill-transfer dimension, by contrast, is harder to standardize and more dependent on coach competence, and so remains more costly to scale without dilution.

The relational function

If there was one theme that emerged consistently across interviews, it was the importance implementers place on trust. Regardless of differences in program model, geography, or delivery modality, respondents repeatedly emphasized that coaches are most effective when they are able to build strong relationships with participants over time. This was reflected in recruitment criteria that prioritized empathy, listening skills, communication, and familiarity with local communities.

Many implementers described coaches not only as sources of guidance, but also as reliable points of contact for participants navigating periods of uncertainty, setbacks, or personal challenges. Coaches were often expected to adapt program content to individual circumstances, connect participants with external services, and provide encouragement throughout the program journey. Several organizations therefore placed particular emphasis on recruiting coaches from within the communities they serve, arguing that shared language, culture, and lived experience help establish trust and strengthen participant engagement.

The importance attached to these relational dimensions helps explain why many organizations remain cautious about replacing in-person engagement with digital alternatives. While technology is increasingly used to support training, monitoring, and communication, respondents consistently viewed relationship-building, trust, and personalized support as functions that continue to benefit from direct human interaction. This also helps explain the emphasis placed on coach continuity, manageable caseloads, and local embeddedness across a wide range of programs. As a result, substituting technology for in-person contact, or rotating coaches, becomes riskier than it appears. This is the function implementers are most adamant cannot be digitized.

The administrative function

Across programs, coaches are responsible for a substantial range of administrative activities alongside their participant-facing roles. These responsibilities typically include maintaining case records, monitoring participant progress, documenting program milestones, completing reporting requirements, and facilitating referrals to other services. As graduation programs have expanded, these tasks have become increasingly formalized through digital monitoring systems, mobile applications, and integrated management information platforms.

Interviews suggest that administrative responsibilities occupy a significant share of coach time and are often viewed as necessary for program accountability, supervision, and learning. At the same time, respondents frequently highlighted the tension between reporting requirements and participant engagement. Several implementers noted that extensive documentation demands can reduce the time available for direct interaction with participants and increase coach workloads.

Consequently, many recent innovations have focused on streamlining administrative processes through technology-based solutions. Digital tools are being used to simplify data collection, improve case management, support supervisory oversight, and reduce duplication in reporting. Unlike other coaching functions, administrative activities were consistently identified as an area where technology can improve efficiency without fundamentally changing the nature of the coach-participant relationship.

However, as implementers strive to reduce this load, they should also be attuned to the possibility that some degree of administrative activities could actually support the psychosocial functions of coaching – perhaps by nudging coaches to objective indicators of participants’ progress on graduation goals or sensitizing coaches to their own inputs, such as referrals to services. Therefore, identifying the optimal level of administrative engagement for coaches could be evaluated directly.

The prominence of these efforts suggests that many organizations view administrative functions as necessary but distinct from the developmental aspects of coaching. Consequently, a recurring objective across programs is to reduce administrative burden where possible in order to protect time for participant engagement and support. Much of the cost-saving innovation documented later in this report is, in effect, an attempt to strip the administrative load away from coaches so that their scarce relational time is protected.

From functions to choices

Each function implies a different answer to the questions that shape program design: whom to recruit, what to train, how frequently coaches should engage with participants, and which activities can be supported through technology. Programs facing similar constraints often make different choices across these dimensions, reflecting different assumptions about the mechanisms through which coaching contributes to participant outcomes. The following sections examine how these assumptions are reflected in decisions relating to recruitment, content, training, delivery, and cost. Figure 2 provides an overview of this framework by linking each coaching function to its practical expression, the mechanisms that may underpin it, and the design choices it informs.

Coach Profile and Recruitment

“[There is] a trade-off to reach scale. So in the end, you have to strike a balance between having people that are good enough [on technical capabilities] to deliver a good program” - IMPL.2

Key questions addressed in this section:

  • What makes an effective coach?

  • How do different recruitment profiles optimize for different coaching functions?

  • How do programs find, select and retain coaches?

  • What drives coach burnout or retention?

How a program recruits its coaches is a signal—often unintentional—of its theory of change. These assumptions are encoded early in the coaching process when two critical decisions about coach recruitment profiles and hiring are determined (Outlined in Table 1 below). The first decision relates to the target coach profile: the attributes a program treats as essential in a coach reveal which of the key coaching functions it is betting on to carry impact. The second is about process and institutional control: who does the hiring, how selection scales, and how coaches are paid and retained, all of which determine how faithfully a program can recruit for the functions it prioritizes. While these two decisions are often taken simultaneously, and in the process conflated, they nonetheless face different constraints. In the following section, we address them sequentially before turning to a third, often-neglected question — what the coaching role demands of the coaches themselves.

Profile: What Makes for an Effective Coach

Coaches are the individuals selected to support participants on their journey toward self-sufficiency through personalized guidance and mentorship. They serve as a bridge between participants and program resources, help participants navigate challenges and adopt new behaviors, and support them in pursuing economic and social goals. In BRAC's original approach, coaches were high-potential individuals from rural Bangladeshi communities who embarked on a parallel journey alongside the participants they served, which is a design that deliberately fused the aspirational and relational functions into a single person.

What attributes make a coach effective? Our KIIs afforded unusually detailed views into what implementers actually look for, since published evaluations are typically light on this. Table 1 distils the recurring profile criteria and maps each to the function it primarily serves. A notable pattern emerges: the attributes implementers describe as hardest to compromise on — empathy, the ability to build trust, community embeddedness — cluster on the relational and aspirational functions, while the more technical attribute, basic literacy, is treated as a threshold to be met rather than a quality to be maximized. As one implementer put it: "It's much more important that we find somebody who's passionate and engaged and interested in playing this role. And then we take them through a rigorous training process" (IMPL.4). The revealed logic is that relational deficits are hard to remediate after hiring, whereas technical gaps can be filled through training and specialist referral.

However, with scaling and translation of graduation to different contexts, the criteria for hiring coaches are adapted to accommodate the local talent pool for coaches as well as structure, resource and capacity constraints of local implementers. In current iterations of the graduation model, the profile of a coach varies widely - from volunteers to highly paid civil servants - with the hiring being undertaken either directly by the implementer or their local partners, which can be NGOs or governments (see Table 1 below).

This is demonstrated by an interviewee: “(W)hen we're recruiting mentors, we recruit them from the local community. So they speak the same language, their cousins and aunts and uncles of their community. So they're part of the community. And we think that's a really important piece so that they're geographically close, linguistically close and culturally close to participants in the program.” -IMPL.3

Process and institutional control: finding, selecting, and retaining coaches

The ideal coaches that a program wants to hire and the coaches it can hire are often not the same. This gap is driven largely by institutional arrangements: that is, who controls hiring. For example, the implementing partner Concern was able to employ coaches directly in the DRC, allowing for close oversight and program customization, while in Burundi, coaches operated at the community level and were hired through the local government structures (Concern, 2020). The latter arrangement strengthens institutional embedding and program sustainability — but at a cost: coaches who also hold governmental duties face competing demands on their time and attention, the "marginal mentoring" risk (Ragins et al., 2000), in which administrative and institutional loads crowd out developmental engagement. In other words, direct control over hiring may require trade-offs against sustainability and scale (a tension that reappears in the discussion of cost-efficiency approaches, where layering coaching onto existing government structures is a central scaling strategy).

Three process considerations shape how well a program can recruit for its intended profile:

  1. Scalability and objectivity of recruitment methods. Transparent, structured recruitment processes help reduce bias and political influence while supporting scale. Common screening and selection approaches include written assessments, interviews, role-playing exercises, and local outreach. These methods also allow programs to assess the interpersonal competencies they value most, such as empathy, communication, adaptability, and conflict management.

  2. Adaptation to the local talent pool. In some contexts, candidates with advanced qualifications or specialized experience may be scarce. Programs can respond by prioritizing candidates with strong foundational skills and local knowledge, while providing additional training, supervision, and access to specialist support where technical expertise is required. This reflects a broader trade-off observed across programs between technical qualifications and relational competencies.

  3. Remuneration and retention. Compensation structures influence a program's ability to attract and retain coaches over time. Volunteer and low-stipend models may be suitable in some settings but can present challenges for long-term retention. More formal employment arrangements often provide greater stability, motivation, and professional recognition, although they may increase costs. Partnerships with government agencies can provide access to a more established workforce, but coaches may also face competing responsibilities that affect the time available for participant engagement.

As Trickle Up observed, "Finding, training and retaining field staff will be one of the biggest challenges of scaling up" (Abrams, 2012). Coach recruitment should be understood not as a one-time hiring exercise, but as an ongoing challenge encompassing workforce availability, selection, training, and retention. A coach can be selected for the warmth that sustains accountability and then taught the agricultural or financial content she will convey. This is why implementers feel able to prioritize soft skills without anxiety about technical gaps: the part of the behavioral function that is hard to teach (showing up, holding someone to a commitment, being believed) overlaps with the relational attributes they screen for, while the part that is teachable (the content) can wait for training. Recruitment, in other words, optimizes for the functions that cannot be manufactured later. The box below illustrates how different organizations have addressed these considerations across three implementation contexts within a single portfolio.

Coaches as Beneficiaries

“These are intensive jobs, mentally and physically,” Carine noted. “It’s not a job you can do 15 years; maybe 3-4 years at the most.” (Abrams, 2012)

The retention problem also points to something deeper and largely unexamined: the personal toll the role takes on coaches. This matters for two reasons. As a matter of equity, coaches are drawn from poor and near-poor communities, and what they gain from the role is a legitimate welfare question in its own right. More instrumentally for funders, coach well-being is a program-sustainability issue — if the role burns people out in three to four years, the deep expertise and accumulated trust on which the relational and aspirational functions depend are continually lost to turnover.

High rates of burnout and turnover tend to emerge wherever emotional and administrative demands persistently exceed available support and recovery (Bakker & Demerouti, 2007). Coaching involves sustained emotional engagement with highly vulnerable people — a prototypical case of emotional labor (Hochschild, 1983). Moreover, heavy procedural and administrative demands alongside poor compensation models may also strain the role’s sustainability (and therefore cost-effectiveness), as those on minimal stipends (or voluntary roles) may be quicker to exit the role entirely, taking their accumulated trust with them.

In contrast, coaches are more likely to sustain engagement when the role supports autonomy, competence, and relatedness – essentially, nourishing the coaches’ own sense of agency alongside the agency of the beneficiaries they support (see Deci et al., 2017, for a review of self-determination theory applications in work organizations). In the traditional graduation model in Bangladesh, coaches were highly trained and valued as changemakers. They underwent extensive training (up to six months), were given opportunities for shadowing seasoned coaches, and had long tenures, which allowed for deep expertise and trust-building in the community. This shift — away from the highly trained, long-tenured coach toward non-specialist staff on shorter tenures and uncertain pay — is also what makes the role more vulnerable to turnover.

While there is some anecdotal evidence, there are no systematic studies that evaluate the program’s impact on coaches or how coaches’ own professional development may benefit program goals. Our KIIs suggest that non-specialist coaches are often recruited from local communities with experience as community organizers in the context of various donor-funded projects. Experience in coaching roles might elevate their profiles and potential to apply for higher paid positions in the future. When coaches are hired as employees in governmental organizations, they not only benefit in the form of higher wages and access to benefits, but also have opportunities for a more sustained career trajectory.

The practical implication is that coach well-being, manageable caseloads and administrative loads, peer-support structures, fair remuneration, and visible career pathways are not peripheral HR concerns but design parameters bearing directly on coaching quality and program impact and cost-effectiveness. A systematic study of coaches' career pathways, retention, and well-being remains one of the clearest evidence gaps in the field — and, as we argue in the recommendations and research agenda, one that should be tracked as a program-level outcome in its own right.

Program Design: Adaptations in Coaching Content, Training and Delivery

Key Questions addressed in this section:

  • How is the coaching content selected and adapted?

  • How are coaches prepared?

  • How is coaching delivered at scale?

Program design addresses the content delivered by coaches, how they are trained in the content and finally the mode of delivery. Each of these three decision points, like recruitment, encodes an implicit bet on which coaching function does the work. Content choices reveal whether a program treats coaching as knowledge transfer or as something more relational; training choices reveal how much it believes coach competence matters; and delivery choices — frequency, caseload, individual versus group — reveal its working assumption about the minimum effective dose of human contact.

What coaches deliver: content and its adaptation

“Topics are built in a modular manner so that we are able to move them around and still deliver the entire 150 weeks because seasons change. I might start a program in January. I might start a program in October, but seasonal agriculture will start only in July. So, we have built it in a modular manner so this coaching happens today.” - IMPL.5

In the original BRAC Bangladesh program, topics covered twelve areas that focused on public health, education, and social protection, emphasizing the prevention of harmful practices like early marriage, dowry, and human trafficking. They also highlighted the importance of healthcare, nutrition, disaster preparedness, and legal protections for overall well-being. As programs have evolved to countries with different needs (such as the role of GBV or HIV awareness) with different target populations (refugees or urban residents), the topics for coaching have also had to evolve and adapt to incorporate these needs.

Across the graduation programs, the following themes emerged regarding coaching content themes, modularity, contextualization and delivery. Essential content themes often target beneficiaries’ core competencies – life skills like goal setting and resilience – as well as awareness building on topics like environmental sustainability and prevention of sexual exploitation. Most graduation-style programs now begin with a template for coaching that covers several core themes critical to building beneficiary self-efficacy and agency. These cross-cutting themes support the overarching goal of more holistic human development through enhanced food security, savings, business development, and child development.

Content Modularity. While some programs may work with timelines synced for all program participants, continuous government-led programs such as the one in Bihar with Nudge Foundation need to accommodate onboarding of participants into the program at various points of the year. In this case, the coaching content needs to be modular such that coaches can easily adapt to the coaching cycle of the respective participants, e.g. content on farming practices might need to align with farming cycles. This should be possible at minimal effort from the coaches’ perspective.

Content Contextualization

Standardized modules are then contextualized to ensure the languages, cultural references, messaging and applications account for the program participants’ specific needs and local conditions. Therefore, coaches are encouraged to localize the mentoring style and coaching messages that draw from real-life examples, which resonate with participants’ day-to-day experiences. They are also expected to be well informed about the local network of services — including health centers, schools, child protection services, and community safeguarding points — so they can refer participants and their families to specialized support if needed.

Content delivery modalities also need to be adapted to the setting and population (as illustrated by the case of urban populations where home visits may not always be feasible). Alternative communication channels—such as technology or meetings at workplaces or central locations—and flexible, after-hours scheduling should be considered. Additionally, program planning must also address different governance structures, and urban cost variations. For example, in the case of Concern’s adaptations in Kenya, technology solutions were integrated for reaching urban populations in a more efficient manner while in Haiti, coaching visits had to be conducted every 6 weeks, with shorter sessions and simplified messaging for the time-constrained urban population.

How coaches are prepared: training models

“So, I think ultimately, what I hope for is that we end up with maybe a body of the government that already trains (a university), or an NGO if available in the country that has that capacity…And then, we make all of the service providers that are involved in delivering the function, get [a] training on what it means to work with this cohort.” IMPL.1

Coach training is typically organized by program implementers, many of whom draw on BRAC guidance and materials while adapting or developing modules for their own contexts. This combination of shared foundations and locally developed content can support innovation and responsiveness to program needs. At the same time, it may result in some duplication of effort and variation in training approaches and delivery. Greater coordination—such as sharing materials, pooling technical resources, or using common training platforms—could help reduce duplication and strengthen consistency, while preserving scope for contextual adaptation.

Training programs can vary significantly in terms of content, modality and accompanying teaching tools. Traditional training consisted of one-shot, front-loaded versions where coaches are trained intensively before coaching activities begin. This model can be less resource-intensive and attractive to organizations operating in traditional styles. However, new innovations in training have led to digitally aided versions synchronized with the overall graduation timeline, which are gaining increased popularity. As noted by Sumanthiran and Roelen (2023), program resources play an important role in determining the type of training offered and the types of tools used in the training delivery with a strong correlation between the two as illustrated in Figure 3 below.

Figure 3: Training and Resource Trade-off

Source: Authors’ visualization.

  • Synchronous Training. This allows coaches to receive targeted “just-in-time training” before they deliver specific sessions to participants, ensuring that information is fresh and actionable. Most programs include refresher sessions to reinforce learning and adapt to evolving program needs.

  • Digital Tools. Using digital aid can lead to more cost-effective ways of implementing programs. Some examples include the following: tablet- and app-based modules that work offline and sync when connected; online training increasingly supported by AI (e.g. chatbots) for quick answers; and pre-recorded video that serves as a refresher for both coaches and participants.

  • Hybrid training modality. Coaches are trained using a mix of digital and in-person methods, which allows for scalability, while in-person workshops ensure hands-on learning and stronger engagement.

  • Refresher training sessions. This is necessary to keep materials current. When working with the government, training programs are typically residential but can be run at a decentralized level or supported by digital tools above.

  • Feedback mechanisms. Supervisory spot checks, performance protocols, and digitized M&E — sustain quality and let field coordinators support coaches in real time.

The analysis reveals that the role of coaching in graduation is shifting from coach-as-expert (front-loaded investment in coaching competence) toward coach-as-facilitator (relational and motivational capacity, scaffolded by just-in-time technical support). This is consistent with the recruitment pattern documented earlier — screen for what cannot be taught, supply the teachable content later. This pattern once again highlights but does not answer the open question of whether coach quality or coach presence drives outcomes.
