Fundación Capital (FC): Scaling through technology

One of the key areas of innovation demonstrated by Fundación Capital (FC) is the utilization of digital tools to improve impact, efficiency, and scalability. This is illustrated in how FC has used technology to aid coaches and participants in their programs to achieve scale and overcome challenges such as staff turnover and hard-to-reach households. It developed tablet- and smartphone-based applications delivering training modules directly to participants, designed to work offline and upload data when connectivity allows — in effect digitizing part of the content-delivery and skill-building work that a coach would otherwise carry, while leaving the relational role intact.

Figure 4: Innovations in Coaching: Fundacion Capital

Source: FC online materials and interviews with stakeholders.

How coaching reaches participants: delivery, caseloads, and the group-versus-individual question

“[C]hangemakers [or coaches] are not able to keep track of 80 different households. You know, attention is required and 40 is sort of the ideal number to maintain is what we have learned so far. We have not come across so far an opportunity to increase it to 75 and still maintain the same level of outputs.” -IMPL.3

Delivery is where one of the report's central questions — what is the minimum effective dose of human contact? — becomes a live operational decision, and it is also where the field has the most rigorous evidence to date. We therefore lead with that evidence before turning to how programs manage frequency and caseload.

Individual versus group coaching

The most comprehensive comparison to date, drawing on programs in Uganda (Innovations for Poverty Action [hereafter IPA], 2022a; USAID, 2021), the Philippines (IPA, 2022b), and Bangladesh (Das et al., 2022) and synthesized in Beam et al. (2025), finds no major differences between group and individual coaching in consumption, income, or productive asset value. The three settings were diverse: refugee and host communities in Kamwenge District in Uganda; recipients of the government's 4Ps conditional cash transfer program in northern Negros Occidental in the Philippines; and ultra-poor rural households across eleven districts of Bangladesh, identified through participatory wealth ranking. On cost, group coaching was on average roughly 15 to 20 percent cheaper to implement than individual coaching. There is also suggestive evidence that group delivery may strengthen participants’ social ties, though the difference reaches conventional significance in only one of the three settings (the Philippines). The implication is consequential for the four-function framing: if individualized, one-to-one contact can be substantially replaced by group delivery without loss on primary economic outcomes, then much of coaching's measured effect on those outcomes may run through functions that operate as well — or better — in a group (peer accountability, social learning, shared aspiration) as in a private dyad. However, it does not follow that all functions are group-substitutable: the relational and crisis-response work that benefits highly vulnerable participants may still require individual attention, a caveat implementers raise repeatedly.

Group delivery in practice. Group-level mentoring reaches scale by working through existing business and savings groups. Coaches operate within a hierarchical support structure — reporting to field officers and program managers — and typically manage some 40–50 groups covering roughly 150 households, visiting at least twice monthly while balancing direct support with data collection. Many use tablets running proprietary systems that feed real-time data into platforms such as Salesforce, enabling both standardized monitoring and continuous assessment of coaching quality and optimal session length.

Frequency and caseload

Implementation varies widely in caseload and contact frequency. Recent iterations of coaching typically engage participants once or twice a month, a shift from the weekly model used in Bangladesh that is hard to sustain when scaling across geographically sparse populations. To allocate coaching more efficiently, programs can differentiate "fast" from "slow" progressors and vary frequency accordingly, and use group settings and digital platforms to extend reach. According to a recent report, some optimize coaching investment by frontloading frequency and intensity during the early, most fragile phase of the program and stepping down this intensity as participants progress:

“Weekly engagements were reported to be especially critical during asset transfer, livelihood initiation, and early behavior formation stages, where households face heightened uncertainty and risk of failure. In these contexts, frequent contact enables rapid problem-solving, reinforces learning, and builds the trust necessary for sustained engagement. Respondents noted that intensive coaching during this ‘activation phase’ significantly reduces drop-off rates and enhances participants’ confidence in managing new economic activities.” (Ouko & Abrams, 2026, p. 6)”

Reported caseloads for individual coaching are modest, on the order of 25 participants per coach in Trickle Up's East African refugee programs and up to around 40 in one implementer account, with quality widely reported to degrade as caseloads climb well above this. Caseload, however, is governed less by any single benchmark than by the delivery model (individual versus group), travel burden, whether coaches carry competing institutional duties, and whether a specialist trainer is paired alongside the coach. Group delivery raises the nominal figure substantially: pairing a coach with a community-based trainer allowed AVSI coaches to cover roughly 100 participants across four groups (Trickle Up, 2023), while savings-group models report higher household counts still.

Peer Coaching

Another approach to scaling access to coaching is through “peer coaching” or “peer mentoring.” In this model, informal coaches may be recruited from within the community, or from within the pool of beneficiaries that volunteer to support their neighbors along their graduation journey. While we do not find any systematic analysis comparing this approach to traditional professionalized coaching, some preliminary evidence suggests that leveraging peers to fulfil core coaching functions can be effective within a broader ‘graduation-style’ package (See recent evidence from a graduation-style program that utilized peer-coaching in Malawi; Lerva, 2026). Evidence from Zambia is more equivocal. At twelve months, a training component delivered at scale by community-based volunteers added no measurable impact beyond the capital grant alone, and a training-only arm showed no significant benefits against the control — plausibly because, as the authors note, these volunteers lacked the technical capacity for curriculum delivery (of 140 surveyed, only 53 percent could read a simple sentence without mistakes and 42 percent had any teaching experience). However, the three-year follow-up complicates that picture: consumption gains were larger in the full package than in the capital-only arm, though only marginally so (0.44 versus 0.26 standard deviations, p = 0.07), and more strikingly, over 40 percent of the households that the capital-only arm induced into entrepreneurship had closed those businesses by the endline, while the full package (capital plus peer-led training) held its gains in business ownership (Botea et al., 2023, rev. 2025). In evidence from Nicaragua, Macours & Vakis (2016) found that volunteer leaders who modelled positive investment behavior, reinforced program messages, and organized collective action, produced effects that persisted for years. While more systematic investigation is needed, these findings suggest that peer coaches may be able to fulfil some of the core coaching functions-- particularly the aspirational and relational functions, and potentially even certain elements of the behavioral function (such as accountability) -- however, where training is needed, an unspecialized volunteer workforce may not be well-suited to the task. Just as in other coaching models, implementers should remain particularly sensitive to “caseload” and coaching frequency expectations for volunteer peer coaches. Instead, peer coaches without formal compensation may be motivated by other types of non-monetary incentives and rewards, such as an elevated status or an enhanced sense of social worth in the community. More research should examine peer coaching implementation strategies to better understand what might make this approach succeed or fail.

Cost Effectiveness and Innovations for Scale

“I always feel like technology can reduce costs, but, you know, only if you're actively replacing coaches, and this is not something we're doing…But it's, you know, to release [load of coaches], make them more efficient, which can reduce costs, reach more people, but it's not necessarily like in a huge margin. Right. So I think it's important because people might think that, OK, so if I use technology, my graduation program is going to cost three hundred dollars. ” - IMPL.2

Key Questions addressed in this section:

  • What are the drivers of coaching costs and why is it so hard to compare costs across programs?

  • Which coaching functions can be economized — through technology, group delivery, or institutional layering — and which cannot?

Coaching is often viewed as an impediment to scaling, since the traditional approach was very hands-on – with each beneficiary receiving 1:1 support on a weekly or bi-weekly basis. Given this relatively high expense, budget constraints are a primary driver of how coaching is designed and delivered. Implementing organizations have responded with a range of innovations to try to reduce costs without sacrificing effectiveness — summarized in Figure 6 and described below.

Figure 6: Innovations and Cost Savings

Source: Authors’ analysis.

Building on existing program infrastructures

This approach to cost-saving looks for what features of a “full” graduation model might already be available for beneficiaries through other existing programs and attempts to supplement that which is missing. For example, where government programs have already done the work to identify target beneficiaries and hired program personnel, graduation components like “coaching” can be added to the existing touchpoints with beneficiaries. This was demonstrated in the Panama pilot “Cohesión Social,” implemented by the Ministry of Social Development of Panama (MIDES), the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), and the World Bank, which supplemented existing social assistance programs. The program had low administrative costs because government staff were not paid by the program; instead, the time government officers spent on it was quantified, and leveraged the FAO’s experience with farmer field schools (Andrews et al., 2021).

In a similar way, where specialized trainers already exist within the non-governmental ecosystems, graduation programs can partner with these organizations to provide trainings by leveraging coaches as “facilitators” rather than “providers” of training. Examples of such coordination programs come from a recent pilot of a livelihood program in South Africa in collaboration between the government of South Africa and FinMark Trust supported by BRAC International. Supervisors and specialist trainers provide coaches with on-demand expertise, improving coaching quality without requiring coaches to master every topic themselves.

Leveraging technology for scaling personalization

Participants often progress at different rates and coaching strategies can be tailored to individual needs with the aid of technology. For slower progressors, more frequent in-person interactions may be necessary, while faster learners could benefit from a lighter-touch approach that incorporates digital channels. This method would enable the delivery of information in a more scalable manner, helping to overcome resource constraints while still providing necessary support. It is important to note that building coaching and training platforms may not be feasible for small pilots and require minimum economies of scale to be cost-effective.

Leveraging alternative coaching modalities

Instead of the high-cost individualized, one-on-one delivery, coaching can be delivered in small groups, or through volunteer “peer coaching” models to maximize reach and impact (see “How coaching reaches participants: delivery, caseloads, and the group-versus-individual question” above for more on this).

Leveraging feedback from monitoring and evaluation (M&E) technologies

Some implementers use technology in the M&E to reduce cognitive loads for coaches so they can better manage their caseloads and provide more effective coaching. This can be done through tracking and monitoring, micro planning and “just-in-time” coaching of the staff. The AVSI program in Uganda offers another example, complementing in-person coaching with mobile messaging (USAID, 2021).

Behavioral Science Innovations

Another innovative approach to cost-saving focuses on the specific economic and psychosocial needs that coaches support for their beneficiaries and imagines novel ways of meeting those same needs more efficiently. The logic is that if a coaching function works through a discrete psychological mechanism, such as shifting aspirations or relaxing a self-efficacy constraint, that mechanism may be activated through a more brief, psychologically focused, lower-cost channel than sustained one-to-one coaching. This logic is set out in Figure 7 below, which maps the three core needs a coach typically addresses: facilitating social and behavior change, building knowledge and skills, and providing personalized support and monitoring, against lower-cost alternatives for meeting each need (e.g., community workshops and one-off trainings to app-based learning, peer mentorship, and self-monitoring tools). In a four-arm trial layered onto Niger's national cash transfer program, adding a relatively inexpensive psychosocial package (community sensitization through a film screening and guided group discussion on aspirations and social norms, plus a week-long life-skills training) to coaching and savings support improved the cost-effectiveness of the overall intervention, with the psychosocial arm delivering returns comparable to the far costlier capital grant (Bossuroy et al., 2022). Building on the same program, Thomas et al. (2025) show that such gains are larger when these interventions are also "culturally wise," that is, designed to support uptake of new behaviors while operating within the local culture’s own existing set of norms and values.

Figure 7: Needs-centric model for Coaching and Training

Source: Catherine Thomas, Innovations in Coaching and Training, 2023, unpublished presentation.

Box

Novel Tool to Assess Variations in Cost of Implementation Across Contexts

The Quick Costing Tool, developed by the PEI Program and presented in the State of the Economic Inclusion Report 2021: The Potential to Scale (Andrews et al., 2021), allows donors and program implementers to unpack the cost of various economic inclusion programs. It was field tested in 34 EI programs with self-reported costing data. The exercise was conducted in different contexts with varying program modalities. The Panama pilot sits at the lower bound of the range: coaching and skills training together accounted for about 10 percent of program cost — 5 percent each — or roughly USD 200 of the USD 1,825 total cost per beneficiary household.

Figure 8: Variations in Costing Components in Different Contexts

Source: Calculations based on data from Chaudhary et al. (2022).

The cross-program comparison highlights two limitations in comparing costs of coaching across programs and contexts:

Resources of implementation partners

There are a wide range of costing models that depend on program context and the nature and number of implementing partners. The share spent on coaching alone ranges from 5 percent in Panama to 27 percent in Peru’s Haku Wiñay program. This makes the comparability of costing across programs complex. As graduation programs get adapted into existing or new government programs, the challenges to ascertaining the cost of coaching increase with staff working across multiple projects.

Lack of systematic reviews

Andrews et al. (2021) collected costing data on 34 programs, but found that impact evaluation results are available for only one. The lack of data on program costing makes it challenging to conduct value-for-money analysis.

Policy Recommendations from the Field

“We are huge advocates [of cash only transfers], but I think that it creates a long and lasting effect when it comes with coaching and graduation….The key aspect of graduation is coaching and the human touch, especially if you're working with very vulnerable people. …Are you willing to replace the in-person contact of coaches with participants with technology? No, I don't think this is the idea. We still think that in-person contact builds trust, builds a relationship that is important for people that are in this situation.”- IMPL.1

Key Question addressed in this section:

  • What policy recommendations can we learn from the current landscape of coaching in graduation-style program design?

As the graduation approach gets translated, adapted and scaled in different country contexts, content and delivery of the coaching component needs to be flexible to be effective and impactful.

1. Design programs around an explicit theory of how coaching changes participant behavior.

Programs currently differ widely in coaching frequency, content, modality, and coach profile. These differences often reflect varying assumptions about the ways coaching contributes to participant outcomes, whether through aspiration formation, accountability, skill transfer, emotional support, or sustained relational engagement. These functions may have different implications for scalability, technology use, and coach competencies. Implementers and funders should clearly articulate how they view the core function(s) of coaching within their programs and ensure that recruitment, training, content, and delivery approaches align with those objectives. Doing so can strengthen both program design and the interpretation/evaluation of program outcomes to help improve future program design.

Policy implication: Program design documents should clearly articulate the theory-of-change for the coaching component, identifying the primary mechanisms through which coaching is expected to produce participant outcomes and the design choices that follow from that theory.

2. Preserve the dimensions of human contact that current evidence suggests are least substitutable, while adapting modality and intensity to context.

The most consistent finding across implementer interviews and existing evaluations is that some form of sustained relational engagement appears central to participant trust, persistence, and follow-through, particularly among highly vulnerable populations. What is increasingly clear, however, is that historical assumptions about the necessary frequency (weekly), modality (in-person, individual home visit), and duration (multi-year intensive) of this contact may be more flexible than originally believed. The Beam et al. (2025) evidence from Uganda, the Philippines, and Bangladesh, for example, suggests that group-based delivery yields outcomes comparable to individual coaching on consumption, income, and productive asset value. A recent practitioner synthesis from the End Ultra Poverty Global Collaborative describes a staged-intensity model that concentrates coaching during participants’ initial activation and stabilization—when it is expected to have the greatest impact—and tapers support as they progress (Ouko & Abrams, 2026).

Policy implication: Programs scaling under resource constraints should preserve regular and meaningful human engagement as a core design feature of the graduation model, while allowing frequency, modality, and individual versus group delivery formats to be adapted to participant needs, program objectives, and implementation context.

3. Recruit coaches primarily for interpersonal and relational competencies, supplemented by minimum technical and administrative requirements.

Implementers across contexts consistently prioritize empathy, listening capacity, communication skills, conflict management, and local embeddedness over formal credentials when these are in tension. This pattern is consistent with organizational behavior and behavioral economics frameworks that emphasize the relational and trust-based mechanisms through which coaching may operate. Technical knowledge gaps can typically be addressed through specialist referrals, modular training, and supervisory support; relational deficits are considerably harder to remediate post-hire.

While evidence remains limited on which coach attributes matter most for specific outcomes, current implementation experience suggests that relational competencies warrant substantial weight in recruitment decisions.

Policy implication: Recruitment processes should incorporate structured assessments of empathy, communication, adaptability, and community trust (e.g., role-plays, scenario-based interviews) as primary screening tools, with formal credentials treated as supporting rather than gating criteria.

4. Use group-based and layered delivery models as the default for scale, with individual follow-up reserved for higher-need participants.

The most robust comparative evidence to date suggests that group coaching can achieve impacts on consumption, income, and productive asset value comparable to individual coaching, while reducing implementation costs by approximately 15 to 20 percent (Beam et al., 2025). Group delivery also leverages peer accountability, social learning, and the existing infrastructure of savings and business groups. However, implementers also cautioned that participants facing severe vulnerability, trauma, displacement, disability, or social isolation may continue to benefit from individualized engagement.

Policy implication: Programs scaling within national or regional social protection systems should adopt hybrid delivery models in which group coaching is the default, with structured triage protocols to identify participants requiring supplementary individual contact.

5. Treat technology as augmentation of specific coaching functions, not as substitution for the relational core.

Digital tools such as tablet-based monitoring systems, modular training platforms, AI-supported troubleshooting, interactive voice response (IVR) systems, and mobile messaging can improve efficiency and consistency in program delivery. Implementers report particular value in reducing administrative burden, supporting coach learning, and strengthening supervision. However, the current evidence base does not yet provide clear guidance on which coaching functions can be substituted through digital channels without diminishing impact. Emerging experience suggests that administrative, informational, and monitoring functions may be more amenable to digitization than relational and aspirational functions.

Policy implication: Investment in digital tools should focus on functions where evidence and implementation experience suggest the greatest potential for efficiency gains, including case management, content delivery, refresher training, and supervisory feedback systems. Programs should continue to prioritize human engagement for relational and motivational functions while experimentation and evidence on digital substitution continues to develop.

6. Where feasible, build continuous, modular, and synchronous training systems rather than one-shot training models.

Implementer experience indicates that traditional front-loaded training, while operationally simpler, struggles to keep pace with the adaptive, multi-stage nature of coaching across an 18–36 month program cycle. Modular, just-in-time training systems, which are synchronized with participant program stage, seasonal cycles, and emerging coach needs, appear better suited to sustaining coaching quality, particularly when complemented by digital refreshers and supervisory feedback loops.

Policy implication: Training architectures should combine an initial intensive grounding with ongoing modular refreshers, supervisory feedback, and digital support tools, rather than treating training as a discrete pre-deployment activity.

7. Manage caseloads explicitly and invest in coach well-being, retention, and career trajectories as a sustainability issue.

Field consensus suggests that approximately 40 households represents an operational benchmark for professional, individualized coaching, with attempts to push significantly above this level associated with declines in engagement quality. Group-based models can extend reach considerably (often to 150 households across 40–50 groups) but create their own demands on coach time, mobility, and administrative capacity. Coaching can be emotionally and operationally demanding, particularly when working with highly vulnerable populations. Practitioners report that multi-year tenures are difficult to sustain, and the field lacks systematic evidence on coach burnout, turnover, and longer-term career outcomes. These are gaps that organizational behavior research suggests may influence both coaching quality and program sustainability.

Policy implication: Programs should establish realistic caseload benchmarks calibrated to delivery model, build in supervisory and peer-support structures, and treat coach well-being, fair remuneration, and career progression as core design parameters rather than residual concerns.

8. Standardize cross-program reporting on coaching design, delivery, and costs.

Cross-program learning is currently constrained by inconsistent reporting on the parameters that most determine coaching cost and effectiveness: caseload, contact frequency, session duration, coach compensation, training intensity, attrition, and per-participant coaching cost. The Quick Costing Tool developed under the PEI program offers a useful template, but it has not been adopted as a field standard. Without comparable data, meaningful comparisons of program costs, delivery approaches, and effectiveness remain challenging – limiting our collective capacity to find the most cost-effective solutions for economic inclusion.

Policy implication: Donors, researchers, and implementers should coordinate on a minimum reporting standard for coaching parameters and costs, and encourage its use across funded programs to strengthen comparability and cross-program learning.

9. Prioritize research designs that identify the active ingredients of coaching.

A central conclusion of this report is that coaching remains one of the most important and widely used components of graduation programming, yet important questions remain about how different coaching features contribute to participant outcomes. Future evaluations should move beyond estimating bundled program effects and seek to examine specific elements of coaching, including frequency, staged intensity, modality, delivery, content, coach attributes, and technology use. Particular priorities include understanding the contribution of coaching relative to other program components, identifying which coach attributes are associated with stronger outcomes, assessing the scope for digital delivery, and examining coach well-being and retention as outcomes in their own right.

Policy implication: Funders should support research designs that generate evidence on which coaching features matter most, for whom, and under what conditions, including longer-term tracking of both participant and coach outcomes.

Appendix

Table A1: The core components of the Graduation Program typically include:

ComponentDescription
Targeting and SelectionIdentifying extremely poor and vulnerable populations needing external support to improve their lives.
Asset TransferProviding income-generating assets like livestock or vocational tools to beneficiaries.
Skills Training and SupportOffering training in financial literacy, business, and technical skills for income-generating activities.
SavingsEncouraging savings to build financial resilience and facilitating access to savings mechanisms.
Life Skills CoachingProviding mentorship to build confidence, problem-solving, and decision-making skills.
HealthcareEnsuring access to basic healthcare services and linking beneficiaries to health support systems.
Social EmpowermentPromoting social inclusion by building networks and encouraging community participation.
Consumption SupportOffering temporary stipends to meet immediate needs without jeopardizing acquired assets.

Source: BRAC 2015

Table A2: BRAC Recommended Curriculum for Weekly Coaching Visits Covering 12 social & health issues

TopicShort Description
Early/Child MarriageDangers of early marriage and discouragement of the practice.
Marriage RegistrationImportance for legal rights and survivorship protection.
DowryNegative impacts and discouragement of the practice.
Human TraffickingAwareness on trafficking risks for women and children.
Disaster ManagementPreparedness for floods, cyclones, and droughts.
Early Childhood EducationImportance of early learning and development.
Family PlanningEducation and promotion of family planning practices.
Healthy NutritionDaily food habits to combat malnutrition.
Vitamin A IntakeImportance of vitamin consumption for health.
Waterborne DiseasesPrevention and treatment of common waterborne illnesses.
De-wormingEducation on de-worming practices for health.
ImmunizationsImportance of vaccines for disease prevention.

Source: BRAC, 2015, p. 67

Table A3: Translation of Coaching from High-Income to Graduation Settings: Moderators

While the parallels between OB mentoring theory and graduation coaching are strong, applying these frameworks to contexts of extreme poverty requires attention to important contextual differences. Table A3 summarizes the main adaptations required when transposing the OB framework from formal organizational settings to graduation programs.

Contextual ModeratorInsights from OB LiteratureImplications for Graduation Programs
From corporations to communitiesMentoring relationships are shaped by sociocultural context - e.g. institutional structures, cultural norms, community dynamics (Chandler, Kram and Yip, 2011).Coaching relationships operate within informal economies & resource-constrained environments. Psychosocial mentoring functions may play a more central role.
Flattened hierarchies and peer dynamicsHierarchical differences between mentor and protégé assumed although peer relationships grounded in trust and mutuality can generate strong developmental outcomes (Kram and Isabella, 1985). Research suggests that empathy and relational competence are critical predictors of effective developmental support (Allen, 2003).Graduation coaches are often recruited from participants’ own communities and may possess limited formal authority or technical expertise. Shared language, lived experience, and relational trust may therefore matter as much as technical knowledge.
Formal assignment versus organic relationship developmentAssigned relationships produce weaker outcomes than organically formed relationships because relational quality is harder to establish (Ragins et al., 2000).Graduation coaching is formally assigned and programmatically structured. Programs must actively create conditions that support trust-building, including careful matching, regular contact, relational training, and manageable caseloads.
Identity transformation and the entrepreneurial self

Individuals adapt to new roles

by experimenting with alternative identities through role models and

Feedback (Ibarra, 1999). Also, self-concept shapes economic behavior (Akerlof & Kranton, 2000).

Coaches play an important role in helping participants develop an identity associated with entrepreneurship, economic agency, and self-reliance, which may be least measured but most consequential outcomes of coaching.
Emotional labor and coach sustainabilityEmotional demands of developmental work exist as demonstrated by burnout when job demands consistently exceed available resources. (Hochschild, 1983; Bakker and Demerouti, 2007) Self-determination theory further emphasizes the importance of autonomy, competence, and relatedness for sustaining motivation (Deci & Ryan, 2000).Sustained emotional engagement with highly vulnerable populations. Coach well-being, manageable administrative burdens, peer support systems, and opportunities for professional development may be critical for long-term program sustainability.

Table A4: Key considerations for coaching in graduation programs

Coaching ComponentStrategiesExamples
Coach recruitment and selection

  • Leverage local partnerships with government or NGOs for staffing and recruitment

  • Establish transparent recruitment guidelines, with clear job descriptions and remuneration

  • Ensure consistency and clarity in coach roles

Training for coaches

  • Tailor training to program timelines (using synchronic vs. front-loaded approaches)

  • Leverage technology to reduce costs and enable “just-in-time” learning

  • Align training with UPG timelines and budget constraints

Balancing trade offs: Coaching frequency and caseloads

  • Combine group coaching sessions with individual follow-ups

  • Use flexible scheduling to balance caseloads

  • Reduces coach burden by leveraging savings/business groups

Evidence and impact monitoring

  • Evaluate both consumption outcomes and other impacts (e.g. productive or business asset value)

  • Research in PHL indicates similar consumption outcomes; further analysis on asset value is needed

  • “And going from pilot to scale is more than just “more of the same.” It’s no longer “a close-knit family” running the program, Carine noted. “You need more checks and balances.” (Abrams, 2012)

Coaching content: Continuous adaptation to beneficiary needs

  • Regularly adapt coaching content to meet the evolving needs of participants

  • Incorporate special adaptations (e.g. psycho-social counseling for vulnerable groups, youth support)

  • Adjust program components based on beneficiary feedback

  • Trickle Up’s India Program adjusted “handholding” visit frequency and emphasized helping women access public services (Abrams, 2012)

Scaling: Leveraging networks and partnerships

  • Strengthen delivery by engaging specialists to reduce coach loads

  • Build coaching peer networks

  • Use tech tools (e.g. WhatsApp groups) for real-time feedback

  • AVSI’s peer network model supports collaborative learning

Optimizing resources: Use of technology

  • Revise coaching tools (e.g. simplify graduation tools with more pictures and clear descriptions)

  • Shorten M&E tools and develop user-friendly coaching materials

  • Use technology (digital/tablet diaries, voice recordings with transcription, IVR systems) to minimize administrative burden

  • BOMA is experimenting with digital innovations to lower operational costs and ease coach workload

  • E.g. “Using Google Meets for daily reviews, daily coaching, daily problem solving.”

Funding considerations: Program cycles and impact tracking

  • Define clear funding periods, timelines, and deliverables

  • Implement longer tracking periods to measure overall impact

  • Ensures that program outcomes are tracked over a meaningful period

Source: Authors’ analysis.
